title: Decide whether a proposed microservice should actually exist
description: Apply structured criteria to decide whether a proposed Notifications service should be extracted from the monolith, kept as a module, or eliminated entirely.

data.text: A team proposes extracting Notifications from the monolith into a standalone microservice. The pitch: 'It scales independently and other teams can use it.' You need to evaluate whether this service should exist, what its boundaries should be, and what the migration cost would be.

terms.definition: A DDD boundary where a domain model is consistent and evolves independently.
A small, shared code or model area between bounded contexts that cannot diverge.
Incrementally replacing parts of a monolith by intercepting requests and routing them to new services.
The ability of a team to change, deploy, and operate a service without coordinating with other teams.
The ongoing expense of monitoring, deploying, and debugging a service in production.

data.title: Every microservice is a tax
data.text: A microservice adds latency, operational complexity, and deployment coordination. If the service does not reduce team coordination or solve a scaling problem, it is pure overhead dressed up as architecture.

cards.title: Extract to Microservice
cards.description: Notifications becomes a standalone service with its own database and deployment.
pros: Independent scaling for high-volume notification bursts
Team can own the full lifecycle without blocking others
Technology choice can differ from the monolith
Failure isolation: notification issues do not crash the monolith
cons: Distributed data management: user preferences split across services
Network calls add latency to user-facing flows
Local development requires running the full mesh

cards.title: Keep as Modular Monolith
cards.description: Notifications remains an internal module with strict boundaries and a public interface.
pros: No network overhead; in-process calls are fast and reliable
cons: Cannot scale the notification sender independently of the web app
Module boundaries degrade without language-enforced isolation
One team's deploy affects all teams using the monolith

cards.title: Eliminate or Use a Managed Service
cards.description: Remove custom notification code and use a SaaS provider (SendGrid, Firebase, OneSignal).
pros: Zero operational burden for delivery infrastructure
Built-in analytics, templates, and compliance features
Scales automatically to millions of notifications
Your team focuses on business logic, not MTA maintenance
cons: Vendor lock-in and per-message cost at scale
Limited customization for complex routing rules
Data leaves your control for compliance review
Abstraction leaks: provider-specific errors surface in your app

items.text: Does it own its own data with minimal coupling to other services?
Does it have independent scaling requirements (spiky traffic, long-running jobs)?
Is there a dedicated team that would own its lifecycle end-to-end?
Are deployment and monitoring budgets available for another service?
Would a managed SaaS solution eliminate 90 percent of the work?
Does the current monolith module have clear, stable boundaries?
What is the estimated extraction cost in engineering weeks?

data.title: Modular monolith: Enforced boundaries with C#
data.content: Using internal access and dependency rules to prevent boundary erosion.

data.title: Microservice extraction: Contract via gRPC
data.content: If extracted, the monolith becomes a client of the notification service.

data.title: Recommended approach: Use a managed service; keep the monolith module
data.content: Notifications do not need independent scaling because they are already async and bounded by third-party provider throughput. A dedicated team does not own them. The correct choice is to keep the Notifications module in the monolith and replace the custom email/SMS implementation with a managed provider. This removes operational burden without creating a new service boundary.

data.title: When extraction is justified
data.text: Extract Notifications to a microservice only if a dedicated platform team needs to own delivery infrastructure, you must support custom delivery SLAs per tenant, or you are building a notification-as-a-service product line.

data.title: Key takeaway
points: Do not extract a service to solve a team-communication problem.
Modular monoliths are the default; microservices are an earned complexity.
Managed services beat custom services when the problem is not your core differentiator.
data.takeaway: Ask whether the service needs to exist before asking how to build it.
